meta.subject: Geography
meta.title: Drainage
meta.intro: Drainage basins, Himalayan and Peninsular river systems, lakes, inland drainage, river pollution and conservation.

objectives: Explain the chapter’s major geographical concepts and processes.
Identify important locations and features on an outline map of India.
Relate physical geography to people, resources, environment and development.

blocks.text: Drainage describes the river system of an area. A river and its tributaries form a drainage system, while the area drained by that system is called a drainage basin.
A water divide is an elevated ridge or upland that separates two drainage basins. The Ambala region is an important divide between the Indus and Ganga systems.

Drainage patterns are influenced by slope, geological structure, rock resistance, climate and the history of landform development. Dendritic patterns resemble tree branches; trellis patterns develop where rock bands alternate; radial patterns flow outward from a central highland.
Himalayan rivers are generally perennial because they receive water from rainfall as well as melting snow and glaciers. They often have long courses, large drainage basins and extensive floodplains.
The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar in the Tibetan region and flows through Ladakh before entering Pakistan. Its important tributaries include the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
The Ganga system begins with the headstreams Bhagirathi and Alaknanda, which meet at Devprayag. Major tributaries include the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Son.

The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet as the Tsangpo, enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang or Dihang and flows through Assam before entering Bangladesh. It carries large sediment loads and is associated with floods and channel changes.
Most Peninsular rivers depend mainly on monsoon rainfall. Their courses are generally shorter and more fixed than Himalayan rivers because they flow across an older and more stable plateau.
The Narmada and Tapi flow westwards through rift valleys and enter the Arabian Sea. The Narmada rises in the Amarkantak region; the Tapi rises in the Satpura ranges.
The Godavari is the largest Peninsular river basin and is often called the Dakshin Ganga. The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow eastwards and form deltas before reaching the Bay of Bengal.
Rivers support irrigation, drinking-water supply, industry, fisheries, navigation and hydroelectric power. Their use must be balanced with ecological flows and the needs of downstream communities.
Lakes may form through tectonic movements, glacial action, river processes, coastal processes or human construction. They may be freshwater, saline or brackish.
Wular and Dal are important lakes in Jammu and Kashmir. Sambhar in Rajasthan is a salt lake. Chilika in Odisha is a brackish lagoon, while Pulicat lies along the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu coast.
Lakes store water, regulate river flow, recharge groundwater, support fisheries and tourism, and provide habitats for birds and aquatic organisms. Wetland degradation can damage these services.
Untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, plastic waste, excessive water withdrawal and floodplain encroachment place pressure on rivers.
Pollution can reduce dissolved oxygen, harm aquatic life and affect drinking water, irrigation, fisheries and public health. Dams and barrages can alter sediment movement and river ecology.
River conservation requires sewage treatment, industrial compliance, efficient irrigation, wetland and floodplain protection, environmental flows, monitoring and community participation.
